From: Andrew Clapham

Well Done! Your first issue is
very professionally produced and
informative.

Before proceeding further I have
just tried the RAM TEST PROGRAM
from Issue 36 P.C.W. [POPULAR
COMPUTING WEEKLY- B.C.] and come
up with "Error in Socket 7".
Having been through OUTLET and
virtually all my lad's games
O.K., but I have had crashes
with for instance Home Accounts
Manager and Money Manager. I
never have any success in
getting MCode from BASIC
listings to work either. [Who
Does? - BC] Do you consider the
test valid and would you

recommend I replace the chip
myself?

How about a "LINK UP"? I should
like to know if you have any
subscribers in the Arnold,
[Nottingham] area who understand

beyond my BASIC! level of

To: Andrew Clapham from Brian

That RAM test omitted the <>
sign between I and 0 on line
2010 and I and 255 on 2020.
Assuming you spotted that then
the other thing about that
program was that it stops at the
FIRST error it finds so if there
were any other chips faulty it
wouldn't show with that test. I
would change the GO TOs to GO
SUBs and add a RETURN at the end
of 2500. The basic principle, of
POKEing memory and PEEKing it
back is reliable. You might run
that program again (with the GO
SUBs etc. I mentioned) and Alter
Line 2500 to PRINT I to show the
actual addresses affected.

I checked the circuit board of
my Issue 2 Spectrum and could
see no markings to indicate
which socket might BE Socket 7.
I have, on several occasions,
fitted completely new memory
chips but have never seen any
socket numbers so you may have a
problem even locating the faulty
chip. Having said that, if you,
or another reader, knows where
you can get a spare chip of the
right type (I seem to recollect
there were 2 slightly different
types in the batch I fitted) and
if you can find the right socket
(you could try the new chip in
EVERY socket, one by one until
you succeed)then fitting the new
one is fairly straightforward.

MAKE SURE THE SPECTRUM IS
SWITCHED OFF AND DISCONNECTED!

If you take great care with the
fragile ribbon keyboard
connectors (ease them gently out
of the sockets in the circuit
board) and take care to avoid
static when handling the chips
(I was advised to stand the
whole thing in a dry, aluminium
sink or stand it all on a sheet
of foil) then it's not too hard.
Ease the chip(s) out VERY gently
using a fine screwdriver at the
ends AWAY from the connector
"legs". Press the new chip in
firmly, squarely and gently
checking that you don't bend any
of the "legs". But, when the
chips are down (tee hee!) if it

doesn't work - send the whole
lot off to be repaired (about
`17!). If you have switched off
your Spectrum and have only
messed around with the RAM chips
you couldn't do much harm. Most
of the repair shops have a
pretty standard charge anyway.
Best of Luck! I ACCEPT NO
RESPONSIBILITY AND MUST STRESS
THAT I HAVE NO SPECIAL TRAINING
IN ELECTRONICS!

Regarding your LINK UP idea - if
any OUTLET reader in Andrew's
area would like to contact us
we'll pass on their address...

     Brian

FROM: CHRIS. CLAYTON

Dear Ron & Brian

Thank you for the first issue ofOUTLET, I think it is first
rate, both the contents of the
magazine, and the way you have
organised the arrangements for
supplying it.

OUTLET deserves to be a great
success. I have felt that a
MICRODRIVE USERS CLUB would be
very worthwhile ..... your
magazine looks like it will fillthat need very successfully. I
will tell any users I know aboutit and I enclose my cheque for
the next six issues.

I have already found your
magazine reviews useful, and
purchased CRASH when I would notnormally have done so, because
of the articles you said were init. With the regrettable demise
of ZX none of the magazines
really interest me ..... your
reviews will help me to identifythose few issues worth buying.

A review of 'fanzines' could
also be useful.

Something which I would
personally welcome would be a
supply of 'clip art' graphics
which could be used in art
packages or similar programs,
for hardcopy printing.

I make a lot of use of TASWORD3
but have just ordered a new
wordprocessor from CARDEX which
will print graphics combined
with text. Trouble is, as I
found after I bought ART STUDIO,which I enjoy using, even the
wizardry of such programs does
not compensate for my lack of
artistic skill! The best I can
do to produce anything of real
use to me is to edit existing
pictures, so a supply of same
would be very handy.

I would also like to see helpfulinformation and advice on the
use of modems, comms software
and bulletin boards. My
inability to find help in
mastering my system has

irritated me a lot over the pastfew months, so could you includethe following item in OUTBOARD.
[OK - see OUTBOARD -BC]

My local supplier, Microsat of
Carlisle, are no longer
supplying cartridges and were
rather annoyed that you had
publicised them without their
permission!

I would find it helpful if more
material could be printed out,
eg. the instructions for using
the character set.

Please feel free to use, edit,
ignore any of the above as you
wish. I look forward to my next
issue.                                     CHRIS CLAYTON

TO: CHRIS CLAYTON FROM BRIAN

Thanks Chris. We'd be very
interested to hear about the WP
from Cardex when you get it. We
have received some literature
from them and have put a message
in OUTBOARD but we'd be very
grateful for an independant
review of the s/ware when you've
had time to assess it. Did you
also order HEADLINER and
TYPELINER? What form do  these
"clip art" graphics take? Are
they normal Spectrum SCREEN$? Is
there more than one graphic on
each screen? I can knock out
some simple graphics but need to
know the final format needed.

As for a review of fanzines, the


only one I've seen is EPROM
which is excellent. I may do a
review of that. Anyone else care
to send in any fanzine reviews?

By the way, it's helpful to step
your line numbers in JOTTER say,
10, 20, 30 etc. rather than 1,
2, 3. If you need to add
anything to what you said
earlier it's easier to insert a
line. It also makes it easier
for us to edit for OUTLET as
often a DATA statement needs to
be split over 2 consecutive
pages.

Sorry about the MICROSAT info
but they've got no right to get
annoyed in my opinion when they
put a quarter-page advert in the


July issue of Sinclair User
offering cartridges for sale and
we try to helpfully pass on that
info only a month or two later.
I'm sure they must still be
getting inquiries and orders
directly from that ad as well as
indirectly thru' OUTLET. Anyway,
we've now removed the item from
OUTBOARD.

I'm keeping in mind what you say
about being able to dump more
text to a printer, such as
program instructions. Anyone
else contributing programs might
also take note. However, it
really needs an option to cover
at least the 3 main types as we
do in this text mode so it does
use more memory to include


such routines. One compromise I
may use in a future program is
to put only the essential
instructions in the program and
put the full instructions in a
separate text file which will
load before the program.

              Brian

TO MR. A.D. CLAPHAM FROM BRIAN

Well, you must be a mind-reader
because we've also been thinking
of a two-cartridge OUTLET and a
disc version. This is a good
opportunity to air our ideas.
We'd be glad to hear what
everybody else thinks.

We are strongly in favour of a
twin-cartridge OUTLET but the
2nd cartridge might be optional.
That is, it would contain no
topical material such as letters
or the editorial so any readers
who wanted to could just get the
one cartridge with no continuing
dialogue or important messages
being absent. You see, possibly
not everyone might be able to


comfortably afford the extra
amount that a 2-cartridge OUTLET
would have to cost even though
we would certainly try to keep
the price as low as possible.

One reason why we would like to
extend OUTLET is because we have
some larger programs, 25K - 48K
which are difficult to justify
squeezing on the one cartridge.
For example, we had a full 48K
adventure program planned for
this issue which we suspended as
it only left room for the
regular features and little
else. Any readers not interested
in adventure games would have
been somewhat disappointed that
half the capacity of the mag was
filled with an adventure!

However, with 2 cartridges it is
much easier to absorb one large
program. Obviously, we cannot
cater to every taste whether we
use 1 cartridge or 2. The best
we can hope for is that every
reader will find sufficient on
each cartridge to justify the
cost. Myself, I think if I got 1
decent little program or utility
for a quid I'd be happy and the
articles, ideas, news, info etc.
etc. would just be cream on the
cake. So with plenty of variety
on 2 cartridges we'd hope that
even if an individual did find a
large program in OUTLET of no
personal interest there'd still
be enough other material in the
issue to stop him feeling that
he'd been ripped off.

Anyway, OUTLET is meant to be an
outlet for you all! What do we
do if a reader sends in a really
nice 35K program? (We should be
so lucky!). That program might
not be to everyone's taste but
it'd be a shame to turn anyone
away. All in all, it seems to us
that a 2-cartridge OUTLET would
be just the right size.

The way we hope it would work
would be as follows: Only
cartridge A would have a "run"
loader and the CONTENTS page.
All items on cartridge A would
be listed on the CONTENTS menu
just as they are now. Items on
cartridge B would also be listed
on the same CONTENTS page
(whether you had bought both

cartridges or not) but they may
be shown in a different INK
colour and perhaps all pushed to
the end of the list. Anyone with
2 drives could put cartridge B
in drive 2. When they selected
an item on cartridge B the LOAD
routine would automatically LOAD
from drive 2. If there were no
drive 2 present it would,
instead, display a prompt:
"please insert cartridge B in
drive 1" (Now you know why I've
been looking for a microdrive
error-trapping routine!).

Another reason in favour of the
2-cartridge OUTLET is that it
would have roughly the same
capacity as other drive systems.
Unfortunately, I have just heard

from a reliable source that the
+3 disc drive is not useable in
48K mode! I've been sitting here
in stunned disbelief absorbing
this information for the past
few minutes! Apparently, this
means that, as much of OUTLET is
written in 48K BASIC and it
would be totally impractical,
and in some parts impossible, to
re-write it in 128K BASIC,
OUTLET will never appear on the
+3! It also means that if you
were thinking of buying a +3
then you could not put any of
your present 48K programs on to
disc! True, you could buy a
Multiface for about `45 but that
is not suitable for saving BASIC
programs and it's certainly not
suitable for OUTLET.

In any event, to begin with, we
have been looking at the Opus
Discovery system as there is a
good user base and OUTLET seems
to transfer directly with no
hassle at all! Regrettably, Opus
no longer make the Discovery and
we are having great difficulty
getting second- hand equipment.
In addition to the Opus, if we
had the spare cash we'd quickly
get two Disciple interfaces +
drives, two Swiftdisc systems,
and possibly two Beta interfaces
and drives. We need two of
everything in case of a
breakdown of course as well as
giving us greater duplicating
capacity.

Our microdrivers needn't feel

their territory is being invaded
-each version would be identical
but would have its own section
devoted to its particular
equipment, e.g.: DRIVECHAT or
any program dedicated to
specific equipment such as a
megaformat routine or whatever.

Remember, the greater the user
base for OUTLET, the more stable
it will become as a long-term
venture and the richer the input
and output.

We'd be glad to hear from anyone
else who'd like to get in their
twopenn'orth on this subject.

Re: the other points in your
letter: We'll drop MDOCTOR from

OUTBOARD - it's a crying shame
that it's no longer available.
Peculiar that Softlink say their
copy is damaged!!!??? Actually,
I've an idea that M/DOC and
MDOCTOR are not the same utility
at all - I vaguely recollect
seeing them both advertised
separately so perhaps that's the
reason that Pipeq had to give up
MDOCTOR as the name clashed with
M/DOC.

128 Manual? Try writing to
Amstrad. Presumably they are now
responsible for support even if
they never manufactured the 128K
Spectrum - they bought the
rights and ought to have bought
the responsibilities. Anyone
else got any ideas?

I don't think Interface 1 or
microdrives are still being made
but I'm not certain. As you say,
the cartridges are still being
produced.

We'll put our leaflet in your
next OUTLET wallet giving
details of other Chezron
programs (We'll do the same for
anyone else who asks but we do
hope to eventually give details
and even demos of our other
stuff in OUTLET).       - Brian.

To: Don Weerasinghe from Ron

The answer is that we do not use
more than 10 characters! The
secret is to use some of the
Spectrum keywords (which the
operating system treats as 1
character) as part of your
program name - this method can
solve your second problem of
identifying the type of file
saved by doing a catalogue, for
instance:

LOAD.."PROGNAME SCREEN$" SCREEN$
LOAD *"M";1;"PROGNAME CODE" CODE

The word SCREEN$ can be entered
from the keyboard in E mode by
pressing the letter K and either
shift key. Similarly CODE can be


entered from the I key, in E
mode, without pressing shift.

Already I can see a worried
frown creasing your forehead. E
mode? What's he talking about, E
mode? Well, Don, one of the
prices paid for buying new
technology is that some of the
good bits of the old technology
can get buried. The single-
character keywords are only
available in 48K mode on your
128K+2 and, as I recall, the
manual for the 128K model does
not mention the different
facilities available in 48K.

Each key can perform up to 6
different functions in 48K, for
example: Set your machine in 48K

mode and you should see a cursor
at the bottom of your screen in
the form of an inverse K. This
is command mode and if you now
press the V key the Basic word
CLS will appear. As you may
realize, this stands for CLear
Screen. Now press your Capshift
and Symbolshift keys together -
the cursor will change to
inverse E - E mode - and
pressing the V key will now
produce the word LLIST. Enter E
mode again and press V but this
time keep your finger on one of
the shift keys and the word
FLASH will appear. Without
entering E mode, press Symbol
shift and V to produce / which,
together with upper and
lowercase V makes up the 6

functions available from that
one key.

It is quite possible that you
are already aware of this but
what you may not know is that
any of the keywords produced by
a single keypress occupy only
ONE byte in memory so it is
possible to produce a "PROGNAME"
such as :

"RANDOMISE SIN FOR CATS AND LET
ME IN"

which only takes up 10 bytes of
memory.

It is using such techniques and
others which enables Brian and
myself to cram so much into


OUTLET. This, incidentally, also
means that you are unlikely to
see OUTLET ever appear in 128K
mode ON CARTRIDGE as I doubt we
could get on half what is
possible in 48K mode. However,
we are intending to make OUTLET
available on disc at some stage
and this will give more freedom
from memory restraints and allow
a 128K version to be created.

  Best wishes,


  Ron Cavers

найдет на каждом картридже достаточно
материала, оправдывающего стоимость.
Лично я считаю: если я получу 1
достойную маленькую программу или
утилиту за фунт, я буду счастлив, а
статьи, идеи, новости, информация и т.д.
станут лишь вишенкой на торте. Так что
при большом разнообразии на 2
картриджах мы надеемся, что даже если
кто-то не найдет в OUTLET интересной
лично для него большой программы, в
выпуске все равно останется достаточно
другого материала, чтобы он не

бы обидно кому-то отказывать. В целом,
нам кажется, что двухкартриджный
OUTLET был бы как раз нужного объема.

Мы надеемся, что это будет работать
так: только картридж А будет иметь
загрузчик "run" и страницу CONTENTS.
Все элементы на картридже А будут
перечислены в меню CONTENTS, как и
сейчас. Элементы на картридже B также
будут перечислены на той же странице
CONTENTS (независимо от того, купили вы
оба картриджа или нет), но они могут
быть выделены другим цветом INK и,
возможно, все смещены в конец списка.
У кого есть 2 дисковода, могут вставить
картридж B во второй. При выборе
элемента с картриджа B программа
загрузки будет автоматически считывать
его со второго дисковода. Если второго
дисковода нет, вместо этого появится
подсказка: "пожалуйста, вставьте
картридж B в дисковод 1" (Теперь вы
понимаете, почему я искал программу
перехвата ошибок для микродрайва!).

совершенно непрактично, а кое-где и

думали о покупке +3, то вы не сможете

Ответ Don Weerasinghe от Ron:

стве части имени программы неко-
торые ключевые слова Spectrum
(которые операционная система
считает за 1 символ) — этот
метод может решить и вашу вторую
проблему с определением типа
сохраненного файла при просмотре
каталога, например:

LOAD.."PROGNAME SCREEN$" SCREEN$
LOAD *"M";1;"PROGNAME CODE" CODE

Слово SCREEN$ можно ввести с
клавиатуры в режиме E, нажав
букву K и любую клавишу shift.
Точно так же CODE можно ввести


клавишей I в режиме E, без
нажатия shift.

Я уже вижу, как вы озадаченно
хмурите лоб. Режим E? О каком
еще режиме E он говорит? Что ж,
Don, расплата за покупку новой
техники такова: некоторые удач-
ные находки старой технологии
оказываются похоронены. Односим-
вольные ключевые слова доступны
на вашем 128K+2 только в режиме
48K, а руководство к модели
128K, насколько я помню, ничего
не говорит о возможностях,
доступных в 48K.

Каждая клавиша в 48K может
выполнять до 6 различных функ-

машину в режим 48K, и внизу

инверсной K. Это командный
режим, и если вы теперь нажмете
клавишу V, появится бейсик-
слово CLS. Как вы понимаете, это
сокращение от CLear Screen.
Теперь нажмите вместе клавиши
Capshift и Symbolshift — курсор
сменится на инверсную E — режим
E, — и нажатие клавиши V теперь

дите в режим E и нажмите V, но
на этот раз удерживайте один из
shift'ов — появится слово FLASH.
Не входя в режим E, нажмите
Symbol shift и V, чтобы получить
/, который вместе с заглавной и
строчной V дает 6 функций,

доступных с этой одной клавиши.

Вполне возможно, вам это уже
известно, но чего вы можете не
знать, так это того, что любое

"RANDOMISE SIN FOR CATS AND LET
ME IN"

которое займет всего 10 байт
памяти.

Именно благодаря подобным
хитростям Brian и я ухитряемся
втиснуть так много всего в


OUTLET. Это, кстати, также
означает, что вы вряд ли когда-
нибудь увидите OUTLET в режиме
128K НА МИКРОДРАЙВЕ, поскольку я
сомневаюсь, что мы сможем
вместить туда хотя бы половину
того, что удается в 48K. Однако
со временем мы намерены выпустить
OUTLET на диске, что снимет
ограничения памяти и позволит
создать 128K-версию.

### To: Andrew Clapham from Brian

That RAM test omitted the <> sign between I and 0 on line 2010 and I and 255 on 2020. Assuming you spotted that then the other thing about that program was that it stops at the FIRST error it finds so if there were any other chips faulty it wouldn't show with that test. I would change the GO TOs to GO SUBs and add a RETURN at the end of 2500. The basic principle, of POKEing memory and PEEKing it back is reliable. You might run that program again (with the GO SUBs etc. I mentioned) and Alter Line 2500 to PRINT I to show the actual addresses affected.

I checked the circuit board of my Issue 2 Spectrum and could see no markings to indicate which socket might BE Socket 7. I have, on several occasions, fitted completely new memory chips but have never seen any socket numbers so you may have a problem even locating the faulty chip. Having said that, if you, or another reader, knows where you can get a spare chip of the right type (I seem to recollect there were 2 slightly different types in the batch I fitted) and if you can find the right socket (you could try the new chip in EVERY socket, one by one until you succeed) then fitting the new one is fairly straightforward.

MAKE SURE THE SPECTRUM IS SWITCHED OFF AND DISCONNECTED!

If you take great care with the fragile ribbon keyboard connectors (ease them gently out of the sockets in the circuit board) and take care to avoid static when handling the chips (I was advised to stand the whole thing in a dry, aluminium sink or stand it all on a sheet of foil) then it's not too hard. Ease the chip(s) out VERY gently using a fine screwdriver at the ends AWAY from the connector "legs". Press the new chip in firmly, squarely and gently checking that you don't bend any of the "legs". But, when the chips are down (tee hee!) if it doesn't work — send the whole lot off to be repaired (about `17!). If you have switched off your Spectrum and have only messed around with the RAM chips you couldn't do much harm. Most of the repair shops have a pretty standard charge anyway. Best of Luck! I ACCEPT NO RESPONSIBILITY AND MUST STRESS THAT I HAVE NO SPECIAL TRAINING IN ELECTRONICS!

Regarding your LINK UP idea — if any OUTLET reader in Andrew's area would like to contact us we'll pass on their address...

Brian

### TO MR. A.D. CLAPHAM FROM BRIAN

Well, you must be a mind-reader because we've also been thinking of a two-cartridge OUTLET and a disc version. This is a good opportunity to air our ideas. We'd be glad to hear what everybody else thinks.

We are strongly in favour of a twin-cartridge OUTLET but the 2nd cartridge might be optional. That is, it would contain no topical material such as letters or the editorial so any readers who wanted to could just get the one cartridge with no continuing dialogue or important messages being absent. You see, possibly not everyone might be able to comfortably afford the extra amount that a 2-cartridge OUTLET would have to cost even though we would certainly try to keep the price as low as possible.

One reason why we would like to extend OUTLET is because we have some larger programs, 25K - 48K which are difficult to justify squeezing on the one cartridge. For example, we had a full 48K adventure program planned for this issue which we suspended as it only left room for the regular features and little else. Any readers not interested in adventure games would have been somewhat disappointed that half the capacity of the mag was filled with an adventure!

However, with 2 cartridges it is much easier to absorb one large program. Obviously, we cannot cater to every taste whether we use 1 cartridge or 2. The best we can hope for is that every reader will find sufficient on each cartridge to justify the cost. Myself, I think if I got 1 decent little program or utility for a quid I'd be happy and the articles, ideas, news, info etc. etc. would just be cream on the cake. So with plenty of variety on 2 cartridges we'd hope that even if an individual did find a large program in OUTLET of no personal interest there'd still be enough other material in the issue to stop him feeling that he'd been ripped off.

Anyway, OUTLET is meant to be an outlet for you all! What do we do if a reader sends in a really nice 35K program? (We should be so lucky!). That program might not be to everyone's taste but it'd be a shame to turn anyone away. All in all, it seems to us that a 2-cartridge OUTLET would be just the right size.

The way we hope it would work would be as follows: Only cartridge A would have a "run" loader and the CONTENTS page. All items on cartridge A would be listed on the CONTENTS menu just as they are now. Items on cartridge B would also be listed on the same CONTENTS page (whether you had bought both cartridges or not) but they may be shown in a different INK colour and perhaps all pushed to the end of the list. Anyone with 2 drives could put cartridge B in drive 2. When they selected an item on cartridge B the LOAD routine would automatically LOAD from drive 2. If there were no drive 2 present it would, instead, display a prompt: "please insert cartridge B in drive 1" (Now you know why I've been looking for a microdrive error-trapping routine!).

Another reason in favour of the 2-cartridge OUTLET is that it would have roughly the same capacity as other drive systems. Unfortunately, I have just heard from a reliable source that the +3 disc drive is not useable in 48K mode! I've been sitting here in stunned disbelief absorbing this information for the past few minutes! Apparently, this means that, as much of OUTLET is written in 48K BASIC and it would be totally impractical, and in some parts impossible, to re-write it in 128K BASIC, OUTLET will never appear on the +3! It also means that if you were thinking of buying a +3 then you could not put any of your present 48K programs on to disc! True, you could buy a Multiface for about £45 but that is not suitable for saving BASIC programs and it's certainly not suitable for OUTLET.

In any event, to begin with, we have been looking at the Opus Discovery system as there is a good user base and OUTLET seems to transfer directly with no hassle at all! Regrettably, Opus no longer make the Discovery and we are having great difficulty getting second-hand equipment. In addition to the Opus, if we had the spare cash we'd quickly get two Disciple interfaces + drives, two Swiftdisc systems, and possibly two Beta interfaces and drives. We need two of everything in case of a breakdown of course as well as giving us greater duplicating capacity.

Our microdrivers needn't feel

their territory is being invaded — each version would be identical but would have its own section devoted to its particular equipment, e.g.: DRIVECHAT or any program dedicated to specific equipment such as a megaformat routine or whatever.

Remember, the greater the user base for OUTLET, the more stable it will become as a long-term venture and the richer the input and output.

We'd be glad to hear from anyone else who'd like to get in their twopenn'orth on this subject.

Re: the other points in your letter: We'll drop MDOCTOR from OUTBOARD — it's a crying shame that it's no longer available. Peculiar that Softlink say their copy is damaged!!!??? Actually, I've an idea that M/DOC and MDOCTOR are not the same utility at all — I vaguely recollect seeing them both advertised separately so perhaps that's the reason that Pipeq had to give up MDOCTOR as the name clashed with M/DOC.

128 Manual? Try writing to Amstrad. Presumably they are now responsible for support even if they never manufactured the 128K Spectrum — they bought the rights and ought to have bought the responsibilities. Anyone else got any ideas?

I don't think Interface 1 or microdrives are still being made but I'm not certain. As you say, the cartridges are still being produced.

We'll put our leaflet in your next OUTLET wallet giving details of other Chezron programs (We'll do the same for anyone else who asks but we do hope to eventually give details and even demos of our other stuff in OUTLET).

— Brian.

**To: Don Weerasinghe from Ron**

The answer is that we do not use more than 10 characters! The secret is to use some of the Spectrum keywords (which the operating system treats as 1 character) as part of your program name - this method can solve your second problem of identifying the type of file saved by doing a catalogue, for instance:

```text
LOAD.."PROGNAME SCREEN$" SCREEN$
LOAD *"M";1;"PROGNAME CODE" CODE
```

The word `SCREEN$` can be entered from the keyboard in E mode by pressing the letter K and either shift key. Similarly `CODE` can be entered from the I key, in E mode, without pressing shift.

Already I can see a worried frown creasing your forehead. E mode? What's he talking about, E mode? Well, Don, one of the prices paid for buying new technology is that some of the good bits of the old technology can get buried. The single-character keywords are only available in 48K mode on your 128K+2 and, as I recall, the manual for the 128K model does not mention the different facilities available in 48K.

Each key can perform up to 6 different functions in 48K, for example: Set your machine in 48K mode and you should see a cursor at the bottom of your screen in the form of an inverse K. This is command mode and if you now press the V key the Basic word `CLS` will appear. As you may realize, this stands for CLear Screen. Now press your Capshift and Symbolshift keys together - the cursor will change to inverse E - E mode - and pressing the V key will now produce the word `LLIST`. Enter E mode again and press V but this time keep your finger on one of the shift keys and the word `FLASH` will appear. Without entering E mode, press Symbol shift and V to produce `/` which, together with upper and lowercase V makes up the 6 functions available from that one key.

It is quite possible that you are already aware of this but what you may not know is that any of the keywords produced by a single keypress occupy only ONE byte in memory so it is possible to produce a "PROGNAME" such as :

`"RANDOMISE SIN FOR CATS AND LET ME IN"`

which only takes up 10 bytes of memory.

It is using such techniques and others which enables Brian and myself to cram so much into OUTLET. This, incidentally, also means that you are unlikely to see OUTLET ever appear in 128K mode ON CARTRIDGE as I doubt we could get on half what is possible in 48K mode. However, we are intending to make OUTLET available on disc at some stage and this will give more freedom from memory restraints and allow a 128K version to be created.

Best wishes,  
Ron Cavers

В том тесте RAM был пропущен знак `<>` между `I` и `0` в строке 2010 и между `I` и `255` в 2020. Я бы заменил `GO TO` на `GO SUB` и добавил `RETURN` в конце строки 2500. Сам базовый принцип записи POKE в память и проверки через PEEK надежен. Вы можете запустить тест снова (с упомянутыми `GO SUB` и т.д.) и изменить строку 2500 на `PRINT I`, чтобы увидеть сбойные адреса.

УБЕДИТЕСЬ, ЧТО SPECTRUM ВЫКЛЮЧЕН И ОБЕСТОЧЕН!
